questions.stem: An upload endpoint has `try { store(file); return 201; } catch (IOException e) { return 503; } catch (AccessDeniedException e) { return 403; }`. `store` declares `throws IOException`, and `java.nio.file.AccessDeniedException` is a subclass of `IOException`. A user without write permission uploads a file. What does the team see?

options.text: A compile error, since the clause for AccessDeniedException is one that no exception could ever reach
options.says: the clauses are tried top to bottom, and a clause below one for its superclass can never run, which javac rejects as already caught

options.text: A compile error, since a single try may not have two clauses for exception types related by subclassing
options.says: separate clauses for related types are fine when the subclass comes first; only a multi-catch forbids related alternatives

options.text: The endpoint returns 403, since the clause for the most specific matching type is the one that runs
options.says: position decides, not specificity: the first matching clause runs, and this order doesn't compile at all

options.text: The endpoint returns 503, since the first clause whose type matches is the one that runs
options.says: that is how clauses are chosen, but javac refuses this order, so the code never runs

origin.section: The First Catch Clause That Matches Wins, So a Subclass Goes Above Its Superclass

questions.stem: An order form parser has `try { return LocalDate.parse(day) + " x" + Integer.parseInt(qty); } catch (DateTimeParseException | NumberFormatException e) { return "bad input: " + e.getParsedString(); }`. `getParsedString()` is declared by `DateTimeParseException`; `NumberFormatException` has no such method. Neither type is a subclass of the other. What happens?

options.text: It fails to compile, since e has the type both alternatives share, which declares no getParsedString()
options.says: a multi-catch parameter is typed as the alternatives' least upper bound, here RuntimeException, so only its methods can be called

options.text: It fails to compile, since unchecked exception types can't be combined in one multi-catch clause
options.says: any unrelated types can be combined; the error is the method call on e

options.text: It compiles, and a bad quantity makes the call throw, since e is checked against getParsedString() at run time
options.says: the call is checked at compile time against e's static type, the shared supertype, so it never compiles

options.text: It compiles, and a bad quantity makes the call return null, since e is treated as whichever type was thrown
options.says: e is not an A-or-B with both types' methods; its type is the shared supertype, and the call doesn't compile

origin.section: A Multi-Catch Shares One Handler; Its Parameter Is Final and Typed as What the Types Share

questions.stem: `void sync() throws IOException` calls `upload()`, which declares `throws IOException`, inside `try { upload(); } catch (Exception e) { failures++; throw e; }`. A second version of the same catch block adds `e = new IOException("sync failed", e);` just before `throw e;`. Which versions compile?

options.text: Both versions, since in each of them only an IOException or an unchecked exception can leave the catch block
options.says: the compiler tracks the precise types only while e is effectively final; after the assignment, throw e throws an Exception to it

options.text: Neither version, since rethrowing the parameter of catch (Exception e) needs a method that declares throws Exception
options.says: an unchanged (effectively final) catch parameter rethrows only the checked exceptions the try block can throw, here IOException

options.text: Only the first, since the assignment leaves e as a plain Exception in the compiler's view when it is thrown
options.says: the first keeps e effectively final, so throw e throws only IOException; the reassigned e is just an Exception, which sync() doesn't declare

options.text: Only the second, since the first rethrows a plain Exception in the compiler's view, which sync() doesn't declare
options.says: the unchanged rethrow is the precise one; it's the reassigned e that the compiler sees as Exception

origin.section: Catching Exception to Rethrow It Keeps the Precise throws Clause

questions.stem: `findCustomer(id)` now reads a cache, so the team removes its `throws SQLException`. Caller A wraps the call in `try { ... } catch (SQLException e) { return Optional.empty(); }`; caller B has the same code with `catch (Exception e)`. Nothing else changes. What does the next build report?

options.text: An error for caller A only, since B's clause also covers exceptions that any code can throw
options.says: a catch for a checked exception the try can't throw is an error, but Exception includes unchecked exceptions and always compiles

options.text: An error for both callers, since neither try block can throw a checked exception any longer
options.says: catch (Exception e) and catch (Throwable t) always compile, because they include unchecked exceptions

options.text: No error for either caller, since an unneeded catch clause draws at most a warning
options.says: a catch for a checked exception the try block can't throw is a compile error, not a warning

options.text: No error for either caller, since a catch clause may name any exception type the code knows
options.says: only unchecked types, Exception and Throwable may be caught freely; a checked type must be one the try can throw

origin.section: A Catch for a Checked Exception the Try Can't Throw Is an Error, Except for Exception and Throwable
